after: ## 1. Stratification and differentiation by class, gender, ethnicity and age
alt: A grid comparing functionalist, Marxist and Weberian theories of class: what class is based on, each theory’s key claim, and the main challenge to or development of it.
caption: Functionalists see class as functional; Marxists as exploitation; Weberians as market position.

after: ## 1. Stratification and differentiation by class, gender, ethnicity and age
alt: Walby’s six structures of patriarchy: paid work, the household, the state, violence, sexuality and culture, with a shift from private patriarchy in the home to public patriarchy in work and the state. Hakim’s preference theory offers a contrasting view.
caption: Walby sees patriarchy moving from the home into work and the state.

after: ## 2. Dimensions of inequality and life chances
alt: Class, status and power each feed into life chances: the opportunities to gain good health, education, housing, income and long life. Disability shows status barriers at work.
caption: Life chances depend on status and power as well as economic class.

alt: Three ways of measuring class: the Registrar General’s scale, NS-SEC with eight classes based on employment relations, and the Great British Class Survey’s seven classes based on three capitals. Below, the conventional household approach is compared with the individual approach.
caption: Each scale measures something different, and gender changes the picture.

alt: Six views of how class has changed: embourgeoisement, proletarianisation, the underclass, the precariat, the death of class, and Sklair’s transnational capitalist class, each with its evidence or criticism.
caption: Sociologists disagree on whether class is fading, splitting or going global.

alt: Three pairs of mobility terms: intergenerational and intragenerational, absolute and relative, short-range and long-range. A timeline of studies runs from Glass (1954) and the Oxford Mobility Study (1972) to Saunders (1996), Breen and Goldthorpe (1999) and Blanden, Gregg and Machin (2005).
caption: Absolute mobility rose, but relative chances stayed unequal.
